title: GPT-6.2 Astra Solves 218-Year-Old Yale Archive Mystery
summary: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra identified the anonymous creator of an 1808 sketchbook in 22 minutes, autonomously cross-referencing period sources to solve a puzzle
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra autonomously identified the creator of a 218-year-old anonymous sketchbook held at Yale's Beinecke Library in just 22 minutes using publicly available sources.
- The model cross-referenced period diaries and letters to attribute the 1808 drawings to French aristocrat Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot, then predicted the location of his personal journal.
- The recovered diary at Cleveland State confirmed Astra's hypothesis with matching handwriting and a June 1808 entry describing sketches at Fort St. Joseph that aligned with the Yale folios.


OpenAI's[GPT-6.2 Astra](https://emergent.sh/learn/what-is-gpt-6-2-astra) has demonstrated a breakthrough capability in non-deterministic research by autonomously identifying the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale's Beinecke Library. History professor Mark Humphries published a case study on November 24, 2026, showing the model solved a 218-year-old attribution puzzle in 22 minutes and one second, a task human researchers had been unable to crack despite decades of access to the same materials.


The discovery marks a significant milestone in AI's ability to conduct open-ended historical research, moving beyond the deterministic domains like mathematics where large language models have recently made spectacular progress, including solving century-old problems like the Riemann Hypothesis and Navier-Stokes equations.


## The Attribution Challenge


The anonymous sketchbook, acquired by Yale from an antiquarian bookseller in 2020, contains 84 pages with 34 pencil, ink, and watercolor drawings documenting an 1808 journey from Montreal to Fort William and back through the Great Lakes region. The drawings depict locations including Sir John Johnson's house near Montreal, Chaudière Falls at modern-day Ottawa, Fort St. Joseph on Lake Huron, and Fort William on Lake Superior, many of which were destroyed only years after being sketched.


The fundamental problem facing researchers was scale and scarcity. While the route depicted was common, with hundreds of canoes and bateaux making similar journeys annually, only a tiny fraction of written sources from that period survive today. Those that do exist are handwritten, mostly un-indexed and un-transcribed, and scattered across dozens of archives in unlikely locations. Without knowing the artist's name in advance, traditional research methods offered no efficient starting point.


## How GPT-6.2 Astra Solved It


Humphries gave the model access to images of the sketchbook along with minimal context, including a suggestion that the artist might be connected to Kendall or Berczy, two figures he'd previously researched. Running on Ultra effort level in goal mode, GPT-6.2 Astra began cross-referencing the sketchbook's distinctive handwriting and travel dates against publicly available primary and secondary sources.


The model identified Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot, vicomte de Chabot (1780-1875), as the probable artist. More remarkably, it predicted the existence of Chabot's personal diary in the Special Collections of Cleveland State University and recommended ordering microfilm copies to test its hypothesis. The aristocrat was a minor French nobleman and Irish landowner whose family had been displaced by the French Revolution, a figure largely unknown to Canadian fur trade historians.


## Verification and Discovery


When Humphries obtained the Cleveland State diary, the evidence was definitive. The handwriting matched the Yale sketchbook's distinctive style, including the characteristic forward-extending capital letters and long-tailed d's that curl back to embrace entire words. Most convincingly, the diary contained a June 18, 1808 entry at Fort St. Joseph stating 'I took a sketch,' which aligned exactly with one of the sketchbook's dated folios from the same location and timeframe.


The discovery represents a major archival find in its own right. Chabot's journal had been overlooked by specialists despite being cataloged in a university collection, and it now provides valuable primary source material for both Canadian and fur trade historians studying the period.


## Release Date and Availability


GPT-6.2 Astra was officially released on November 24, 2026, as part of OpenAI's expanded model family. Humphries had access to the model in late October 2026 for pre-release testing through the ChatGPT Windows Desktop app. The model is described as quirky but highly capable, particularly well-suited to long-running, open-ended tasks that might take hours or days to complete.


During his testing period, Humphries also had the model examine and correct an 8,002-row CSV transcription of a historical ledger, verifying handwritten arithmetic across thousands of quantities, prices, and account totals over the course of a few hours. He noted that GPT-6.2 Astra completed tasks more thoroughly than both GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5 had managed.


## Model Characteristics and Implications


Humphries observed that GPT-6.2 Astra sometimes communicates in an unusual manner, writing backwards-speak or riddle-like answers that initially seem incorrect but prove technically sound. He speculates this communication style may result from post-training optimization toward deterministic tasks like mathematical proofs, creating odd prose when the model must communicate results based on incomplete evidence, a common scenario in non-deterministic research domains.


Despite the communication quirks, the underlying work product remained consistently reliable. The model's ability to develop hypotheses with limited evidence, make arguments based on incomplete historical records, and predict the existence and location of corroborating sources represents a significant expansion of AI capabilities beyond purely deterministic fields.


## What This Means


The case study provides concrete evidence that advanced language models can now conduct autonomous research in non-deterministic domains like history, not just mathematics and formal logic. While the example is narrow, it represents the core process of historical research: source analysis, hypothesis development, evidence synthesis, and predictive reasoning about archival materials. As models continue to improve, researchers may increasingly delegate preliminary attribution work, archival search, and cross-referencing tasks to AI systems, fundamentally changing how historical scholarship is conducted and potentially unlocking thousands of anonymous or misattributed documents currently sitting unstudied in archives worldwide.
